Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

A homemade Santa chimney display uses cardboard and pool noodles, but a roofing expert warns that this holiday craft could put a home at risk.

According to recent reports, the holidays are a great time to put up decorations around the home, either purchased decor or DIY options. Social feeds are full of ideas, but are all of them good or safe?

A recent viral video on a homeowner’s roof made it look like Santa is climbing into the chimney. It’s a creative chimney hack that might appeal to homeowners decorating for Christmas. But placing cardboard and other craft materials on a roof raises some safety concerns, especially during winter.

Learn what a roofing expert states about the potential fire hazards, moisture problems, and safer alternatives.

A post shared by Drew (@thedrewsocial).

Not according to Andre Kazimierski, co-owner and president of HomeHero Roofing, a residential roofing firm in Illinois.

Industry observers note that “That decoration is definitely not wise to be putting up on your roof,” Kazimierski claims. “Not only is it a fire hazard, but it’s likely going to create issues with moisture.”.

Industry observers note that the cardboard and foam used in the decoration can catch fire, especially if they’re close to a working chimney. “Cardboard is flammable, so if it manages to catch on fire, it can then easily spread that fire to your roof,” Kazimierski warns.

In a recent development, chimneys release heat and sometimes sparks, which could ignite nearby decorations. There’s also a risk of cardboard or other materials blocking the chimney opening, allowing smoke or dangerous gases to enter the home. Even if the fireplace isn’t in use, the chimney could still vent another heating appliance.

Sources indicate that rain and snow present another problem. “Cardboard can absorb a lot of water and get really soggy,” Kazimierski claims.

Wet cardboard can collapse against the roof, while the paper covering and other decorations may start falling apart. Kazimierski warns that trapped moisture could also lead to mold, damaged roofing materials, or unwanted pests.

In a recent development, moisture is already a concern for brick chimneys. “Common brick is like a sponge, absorbing water and wicking moisture to the chimney interior,” according to the Chimney Safety Institute of America. “Defective mortar joints or the use of improper mortar or brick can greatly increase the tendency to absorb and convey water to the interior of the masonry chimney structure.”.

A wet cardboard display resting against the chimney could keep the surrounding area damp, adding to existing moisture concerns.

Homeowners who want to decorate their roofs for Christmas should be careful about how they attach decorations. Nails and screws can puncture shingles, allowing water to seep underneath and potentially cause leaks.

Roofing manufacturer GAF recommends avoiding nails or staples when installing holiday decorations. Large displays can also damage shingles or come loose in strong winds.

Climbing onto the roof to install or remove decorations carries its own risks, particularly when the shingles are wet or covered in snow or ice.

Recent findings suggest that for homeowners who want to recreate the Santa chimney decoration, a safer option is to build a freestanding display on the porch or in the yard, away from the home’s actual chimney. Weather-resistant materials will hold up better than cardboard, and a sturdy base can help keep everything in place during windy weather.

If the display includes lights, the National Fire Protection Association recommends using decorations rated for outdoor use and checking electrical cords for damage.

Keeping the decoration at ground level also makes it easier to inspect, maintain, and remove without climbing onto the roof.

California ordered Waymo off freeways after troubling encounters with road crews and police. Here's what happened and how riders are affected.

Driving through a construction zone can be confusing, especially when lanes are closed or police are directing traffic. Waymo’s self-driving cars have run into problems in these situations, too.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 11, California banned Waymo from operating driverless vehicles on freeways following several incidents involving road crews and police. The manufacturer has since stopped freeway rides in other states as well.

Here’s why California stepped in and what the ban means for Waymo passengers.

The California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) said the incidents put construction workers and other drivers at risk.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 5, three Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on Highway 101 near Burlingame, where crews were working. Waymo mentioned no one was injured, and no collisions occurred.

Industry observers note that the next day, another Waymo attempted to pass California Highway Patrol vehicles during a traffic break on Interstate 280. Officers use traffic breaks to slow or stop vehicles, often because of roadwork or a hazard ahead. Drivers must stay behind the patrol cars until officers allow traffic to resume.

Recent findings suggest that waymo had similar problems in May, which led to a temporary suspension and software changes. But new incidents occurred in November.

In a recent development, in April, California approved stricter rules for self-driving cars. DMV Director Steve Gordon remarked the changes would bring “additional accountability for AV manufacturers.”.

In a recent development, the freeway ban doesn’t affect Waymo’s regular street service, although some trips may take longer. Waymo has also voluntarily stopped commercial freeway rides in other states while it looks into what went wrong.

Waymo’s cars use cameras and sensors to monitor traffic, but construction zones don’t always follow normal traffic patterns. The recent incidents showed problems with how the vehicles responded to road closures and police activity.

In a recent development, there’s no date yet for Waymo to return to California freeways. The DMV wants the company to show that its cars can safely handle road closures and police activity before allowing driverless freeway rides again.

In a recent development, waymo claims it’s working with state officials and will continue testing on freeways with trained specialists behind the wheel. Passengers can still book rides on regular streets in the meantime.

DB Ventures had originally filed suit in April, alleging that Beckham’s brand of luxury colognes and fragrances were being sold at gas stations and discount stores in violation of their agreement.

According to the AP, DB Ventures is seeking at least $41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.

Industry observers note that coty told the AP that it strongly disputes the claims and would not comment further on ongoing litigation. Authentic Brands, DB Ventures’ parent firm, declined to comment to the AP.

Beckham, a former Manchester United, Real Madrid, AC Milan, Paris Saint-Germain and LA Galaxy player who captained the English national football team and was knighted in 2025, has built a business career that includes co-owning soccer team Inter Miami.

According to the Sunday Times, he is the first billionaire sports figure in the United Kingdom, having a combined net worth of about $1.58 billion with his wife, Victoria Beckham, a former member of the Spice Girls music group.

A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the threshold for the state’s original charge of a more serious offense.

Sources indicate that warren 37th District Court Chief Judge John M. Chmura, 63, was found guilty of intoxication while driving his Ford Fusion into a parked bus that was displaying hazard lights March 25. But the court rejected the charge of Chmura driving with an elevated high blood alcohol content of 0.17 or greater, according to coverage on Law360.

Novi 52nd District Court Judge David Law noted that Chmura’s judgment had been affected, but he questioned the blood alcohol concentration at the time of the crash.

“This court may think it knows the answer to whether or not this was a high BAC case,” Law said. “But thinking it knows is not enough. It needs to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.”.

Recent findings suggest that A bus driver sitting inside the bus waiting to resume his route was uninjured in the crash. Sterling Heights, Michigan, police officer Jonathan Journeau testified that Chmura smelled of alcohol, slurred his speech and couldn’t maintain his balance.

Industry observers note that chmura’s attorney, David J. Kramer of the David J. Kramer Law Firm, argued that prosecutors could not establish the higher offense because Journeau failed to determine when the judge’s final alcoholic beverage was consumed.

AI investment has been a key component of recent growth, and tens of millions of ordinary Americans own these companies through their 401(k)s. A slower buildout means fewer construction jobs, less demand for electricians and engineers, and slower productivity gains that drive real wage growth.The fiscal picture is dimmer, too. Much of the consequential economic public policy changes of the past two years didn't depend on Congress, and it won’t go forward either. And while the tax-reform legislation passed last year obviously did require Congress, most of its provisions are permanent and won’t need reauthorization.The administration retains broad authority to problem executive orders and roll back burdensome regulations. Cutting that red tape, on everything from energy production to banking, reduces compliance costs for Americans without a single vote on Capitol Hill.Democrats will certainly try to slow that good work. Their leaders are already planning a wave of made-for-cable show trials that will drain time and attention from officials who should be dismantling the bureaucracy. But investigations can only delay regulatory reform, not stop it.The president’s veto is another silver lining that will likely prevent the Democratic Congress from enacting sweeping tax hikes or new regulatory regimes. The worst ideas will hopefully die in committee or an Oval Office waste basket.The economy has weathered worse than a hostile Congress. Ongoing deregulation and existing tax reform are still tailwinds for economic growth while the veto pen is there to stop headwinds as they arise. The outlook might be blue, but it’s not black and blue.

Wall Street delivered its verdict on the blue-wave midterms 48 hours later in the form of a red wave—red ink, that is.

Sources indicate that after a brief relief rally the day after the election, the Dow shed more than 1,800 points, the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 5% and into correction territory, and roughly $2.5 trillion in market value vanished in a single session. Nvidia alone dropped more than 8%.

It has been revealed that market participants watched the collapse of the AI trade in real time—the bet that a massive buildout of data centers, chips, and software would power faster growth, higher productivity and rising wages for years to come. That theory hit the brick wall of an incoming Congress that has AI and data centers on their blacklist.

Democrats, who will comfortably control the Senate and hold their largest House majority in nearly two decades, have been far more hostile to data centers and AI than Republicans have. Several of their biggest wins came in places such as Texas, where local opposition to fresh data centers had been building.

In a recent development, investors can read the writing on the wall: more regulation and taxation, slower permitting, and lower profits for AI and AI-adjacent companies. Since equity prices are ultimately justified by future earnings, adjusting those future expectations down also drove down equity prices.

>>> What’s Really Behind the Call to Regulate AI.

The fallout goes well beyond Silicon Valley. AI investment has been a key component of recent growth, and tens of millions of ordinary Americans own these companies through their 401(k)s. A slower buildout means fewer construction jobs, less demand for electricians and engineers, and slower productivity gains that drive real wage growth.

According to recent reports, the fiscal picture is dimmer, too. With Democrats running both chambers, there is no chance of further tax reform or meaningful spending cuts for at least two years. If a Republican Congress couldn't bring itself to enshrine the DOGE savings into law, a Democratic one certainly won't.

Instead, Democrat leaders are already promising to restore cost-increasing Obamacare subsidies and unwind recently implemented work-requirement reforms for welfare, all of which will layer new commitments on top of deficits already running at levels once seen only in wartime or recession.

Aside from burdening future generations with debt, these perpetual deficits have consequences for Americans today. The government is crowding out borrowing in the private sector, competing with families and businesses for loanable funds, thereby driving up interest rates on everything from mortgages to student loans to credit cards.

Those higher borrower costs fall especially hard on those Americans that are already in debt and behind financially. The flood of government debt issuance also puts pressure on the Federal Reserve to help finance the debt by creating money to pay for perpetual deficits—a recipe for more inflation.

>>> Slowing Data Center Construction Signals the Need for Pro-Growth Reforms.

Unfortunately, a Democratic Congress will also likely offer no help on permitting reform, which is badly needed to build the pipelines, transmission lines and reliable power plants a growing economy requires.

Recent findings suggest that so the outlook is clearly worse, but why isn’t it terrible? Much of the consequential economic public policy changes of the past two years didn't depend on Congress, and it won’t go forward either. And while the tax-reform legislation passed last year obviously did require Congress, most of its provisions are permanent and won’t need reauthorization.

The administration retains broad authority to matter executive orders and roll back burdensome regulations. Cutting that red tape, on everything from energy production to banking, reduces compliance costs for Americans without a single vote on Capitol Hill.

According to recent reports, democrats will certainly try to slow that good work. Their leaders are already planning a wave of made-for-cable show trials that will drain time and attention from officials who should be dismantling the bureaucracy. But investigations can only delay regulatory reform, not stop it.

Industry observers note that the president’s veto is another silver lining that will likely prevent the Democratic Congress from enacting sweeping tax hikes or new regulatory regimes. The worst ideas will hopefully die in committee or an Oval Office waste basket.

Recent findings suggest that the economy has weathered worse than a hostile Congress. Ongoing deregulation and existing tax reform are still tailwinds for economic growth while the veto pen is there to stop headwinds as they arise. The outlook might be blue, but it’s not black and blue.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding blueprint called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a upcoming, modern class of battleship. But delivering it faces significant hurdles. The first is realistically addressing the Navy’s shaky shipbuilding track record. The second is surviving the changed political reality in Washington—made more challenging by Trump’s original plan to name the class of warship after himself.By any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S. Navy. A modern battleship’s firepower, command and control, and data-fusion capabilities have been proven vital in recent conflicts in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian Gulf. Mitigating shipbuilding risks, such as constrained production capacity and the integration of numerous advanced technologies, necessitate a continuous testing regimen that scales up as the ships are built.The U.S. Navy Could Use a Modern “Battlecruiser” WarshipThe unveiling of the battleship comes as the Navy faces the imminent loss of significant at-sea firepower. By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. To blunt this loss, the next iteration of Virginia-class nuclear submarines will carry 28 hypersonic missiles, and the Navy’s unmanned vessels may also begin to carry offensive weapons.>>> The U.S. Navy Must Build the “Golden Fleet”The Navy missed an opportunity to address this firepower dilemma with its aborted CG(X) next-generation cruiser program, abandoned in 2011. These forced aging destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers to continue shouldering the air and missile defense responsibilities for carrier strike groups. Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, however, lack the firepower and crew to fully assume the cruiser mission. The Arleigh Burke-class has 96 missile tubes, against 122 on the Ticonderoga-class, and has limited berthing for the needed staff to manage air and missile defenses for the carrier strike group.In the long term, the Defiant and subsequent battleships are intended to fill this mission and firepower gap. The Defiant, with its added firepower, sensors and crew, will take over the Ticonderoga-class warships’ responsibilities for defending carrier strike groups. The ship will also employ long-range hypersonic missiles in support of carrier air-strike operations to rapidly suppress emerging threats.The combination of capabilities merged in Defiant with sustained high speeds makes the vessel more closely resemble a battlecruiser—a high-speed battleship able to deliver long-range firepower and defend the carrier strike group from air and missile threats. However, recent battle lessons are creating another critical mission.The damage inflicted upon U.S. Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, and its temporary evacuation due to Iranian missile introduces, demonstrates the vulnerability of permanent land-based naval installations to air attack. Moving headquarters to sea is one way to mitigate this danger, and follows a long tradition of numbered fleet command ships. A battlecruiser with robust command and control capabilities can maintain a common operational picture with the warships and unmanned platforms of its numbered fleet, reducing the Navy’s reliance on global communications.>>> To Build the Golden FleetHow the Defiant Can Clear the Political Minefield on Capitol HillWhile battlecruisers are needed now, the United States faces numerous constraints that must be navigated before they can join the Golden Fleet. The high build cost of these ships will likely stir substantial resistance from budget-conscious members of Congress; a bill estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be upwards of $23 billion for the first and subsequent ships costing $18 billion each. There are also serious shortages of skilled workers capable of efficiently building such intricate and substantial ships. Moreover, establishing new or expanding existing shipyards to build these battlecruisers requires working through onerous shipbuilding regulations.Keeping Congress’ support will necessitate reducing the potential for cost overruns and program delays. One way to accomplish this is to use proven technologies and systems in the initial design. Doing this would result in Defiant embracing existing systems to meet its mission requirements the soonest. Integrating systems like the hypersonic missile technologies being developed for the Zumwalt-class destroyers and the new AN/SPY-6 radars being installed in Arleigh Burke-class vessels will further compress production timelines.In time, the design will need to be improved on through continuous updates—one being the transition to nuclear power to sustain high speeds and pace the aircraft carrier the battlecruiser is intended to protect. One option is using the same A1B nuclear power plant now used in the Ford-class aircraft carriers, given enough time for production to ramp up to support aircraft carrier and battlecruiser production.Resurrecting the battlecruiser for modern naval missions is a highly ambitious plan, and it may yet fall through. But it is needed to equip the U.S. Navy with the capabilities for fighting a modern naval war across the Pacific.This piece originally appeared in The National Interest.

According to recent reports, last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding plan called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a upcoming, modern class of battleship. But delivering it faces significant hurdles. The first is realistically addressing the Navy’s shaky shipbuilding track record. The second is surviving the changed political reality in Washington—made more challenging by Trump’s original plan to name the class of warship after himself.

By any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S. Navy. A modern battleship’s firepower, command and control, and data-fusion capabilities have been proven vital in recent conflicts in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian Gulf. Mitigating shipbuilding risks, such as constrained production capacity and the integration of numerous advanced technologies, necessitate a continuous testing regimen that scales up as the ships are built.

The U.S. Navy Could Use a Modern “Battlecruiser” Warship.

The unveiling of the battleship comes as the Navy faces the imminent loss of significant at-sea firepower. By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. To blunt this loss, the next iteration of Virginia-class nuclear submarines will carry 28 hypersonic missiles, and the Navy’s unmanned vessels may also begin to carry offensive weapons.

According to recent reports, >>> The U.S. Navy Must Build the “Golden Fleet”.

It has been revealed that the Navy missed an opportunity to address this firepower dilemma with its aborted CG(X) next-generation cruiser program, abandoned in 2011. These forced aging destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers to continue shouldering the air and missile defense responsibilities for carrier strike groups. Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, however, lack the firepower and crew to fully assume the cruiser mission. The Arleigh Burke-class has 96 missile tubes, against 122 on the Ticonderoga-class, and has limited berthing for the needed staff to manage air and missile defenses for the carrier strike group.

In the long term, the Defiant and subsequent battleships are intended to fill this mission and firepower gap. The Defiant, with its added firepower, sensors and crew, will take over the Ticonderoga-class warships’ responsibilities for defending carrier strike groups. The ship will also employ long-range hypersonic missiles in support of carrier air-strike operations to rapidly suppress emerging threats.

According to recent reports, the combination of capabilities merged in Defiant with sustained high speeds makes the vessel more closely resemble a battlecruiser—a high-speed battleship able to deliver long-range firepower and defend the carrier strike group from air and missile threats. However, recent battle lessons are creating another critical mission.

Recent findings suggest that the damage inflicted upon U.S. Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, and its temporary evacuation due to Iranian missile launches, demonstrates the vulnerability of permanent land-based naval installations to air attack. Moving headquarters to sea is one way to mitigate this danger, and follows a long tradition of numbered fleet command ships. A battlecruiser with robust command and control capabilities can maintain a common operational picture with the warships and unmanned platforms of its numbered fleet, reducing the Navy’s reliance on global communications.

>>> To Build the Golden Fleet.

How the Defiant Can Clear the Political Minefield on Capitol Hill.

While battlecruisers are needed now, the United States faces numerous constraints that must be navigated before they can join the Golden Fleet. The high build cost of these ships will likely stir substantial resistance from budget-conscious members of Congress; a bill estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be upwards of $23 billion for the first and subsequent ships costing $18 billion each. There are also serious shortages of skilled workers capable of efficiently building such intricate and substantial ships. Moreover, establishing upcoming or expanding existing shipyards to build these battlecruisers requires working through onerous shipbuilding regulations.

Keeping Congress’ support will necessitate reducing the potential for cost overruns and program delays. One way to accomplish this is to use proven technologies and systems in the initial design. Doing this would result in Defiant embracing existing systems to meet its mission requirements the soonest. Integrating systems like the hypersonic missile technologies being developed for the Zumwalt-class destroyers and the new AN/SPY-6 radars being installed in Arleigh Burke-class vessels will further compress production timelines.

In time, the design will need to be improved on through continuous updates—one being the transition to nuclear power to sustain high speeds and pace the aircraft carrier the battlecruiser is intended to protect. One option is using the same A1B nuclear power plant now used in the Ford-class aircraft carriers, given enough time for production to ramp up to support aircraft carrier and battlecruiser production.

In a recent development, resurrecting the battlecruiser for modern naval missions is a highly ambitious plan, and it may yet fall through. But it is needed to equip the U.S. Navy with the capabilities for fighting a modern naval war across the Pacific.

This piece originally appeared in The National Interest.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission. At bottom, she argues for implementing a version of the UK Takeover Panel to regulate procedural requirements for proposal submission while leaving decisions about content scope to shareholders. Along the way, she argues that The Heritage Foundation, including by way of its American Investor Initiative, “is having second thoughts” about prior positions Heritage has taken on the issue, and that Heritage “seems distinctly unhappy with the SEC’s direction of travel” and is thus left in “the strange position of defending the very mechanism it spent years arguing had made shareholder meetings too political.” These characterizations of Heritage warrant some clarification.To begin with, we at Heritage certainly hope we never stop assessing past positions in the light of current experience, and that we will always do our best to reflect the latest understanding of the myriad factors impacting policies over time. Having said that, our current view of Rule 14a-8 is not nearly as conflicted as Wilson presents.For example, Wilson contrasts our past criticism of proxy advisers, ESG and “woke investment,” with our current position of cautioning against too hasty rescission of Rule 14a-8. Specifically, as we noted in a recent letter published in the Wall Street Journal, we believe the goal of depoliticizing corporate governance is best served by a “generous grace period” before rescission takes effect.The current mix of corporate commitments took shape over decades in which mainly one set of proponents used the proposal process. Proponents who favor corporate neutrality, Heritage among them, have only recently begun to use the process effectively. Ending it abruptly would freeze in place the results of that one-sided period. A transition period would also allow states to develop their own frameworks for shareholder proposals, give companies and investors time to adjust, and avoid entrenching a status quo that formed under proxy-advisory and asset-manager voting practices that are themselves only now being reformed.While our position may in some sense have shifted from “keep the rule” to “rescind the rule slowly,” the animating principle remains the same: The prosperity-generating power of free-market capitalism must be defended against the myriad conflicts of interest distorting relevant inputs from corporate leaders, asset managers, proxy advisors, activists, and others. Particularly with respect to ESG (including DEI, sustainability, and net zero, as well as the successor labels under which similar commitments are increasingly marketed), resisting the use of corporate and regulatory machinery to advance policy goals that could not be achieved through markets or legislatures is a consistent theme. As has been said: “Every great cause begins as a movement, becomes a business, and eventually degenerates into a racket.”>>> The Case of the Missing Heritage Foundation ProposalsTo illustrate, consider the four justifications most commonly offered for corporate sustainability commitments and investments, and why each, on closer examination, proves incomplete. First, sustainability commitments are often described as a matter of legal compliance. But the leading climate-disclosure mandates, such as California’s SB 253 and SB 261, require companies to report emissions and climate-related risks, not to adopt reduction targets. And when we have offered to withdraw shareholder proposals if a organization would state publicly that its sustainability commitments are legally required, companies have generally declined to do so. That reluctance suggests the commitments rest on something other than compliance.Second, sustainability commitments are frequently defended as risk management, a necessary cost of reducing exposure to climate-related harm. But according to the Global Carbon Budget 2025, the United States accounts for roughly 13 percent of global fossil CO₂ emissions, compared with about 32 percent for China and 8 percent for India. Even if every U.S. corporation reached net zero, the effect on global emissions, and so on the physical risks companies face, would be modest without comparable action elsewhere. Firm-level transition risks, such as regulatory and litigation exposure, may justify some measures. But those risks call for targeted, quantified responses, not open-ended commitments.Third, sustainability commitments are said to reflect client demand. BlackRock’s 2020 letter to clients, for example, justified its sustainability initiatives in part by noting that “more and more of our clients have focused on the impact of sustainability on their portfolios.” Client demand alone, however, does not show that a commitment creates value for shareholders. Demand for a product does not justify supplying it at any price, and sustainability commitments deserve the same discipline. Their costs and benefits should be fully disclosed so that clients and shareholders can make informed judgments.Finally, one would expect companies making substantial sustainability commitments to have done the relevant expected-value analysis and to track the returns. Yet even advocates of corporate sustainability acknowledge that this rarely happens. The director of NYU Stern’s Center for Sustainable Business has observed that “most companies are not monetizing the Return on Sustainability Investment,” and that financial benefits “are tracked differently (if at all) by different units and are not aggregated.” Without such measurement, it is difficult to assess whether these commitments serve shareholders’ interests.If these conventional justifications are incomplete, a further explanation lies in the incentives of the parties involved. Asset managers market ESG products and compete for mandates from clients who want them. Proxy advisors have offered ESG-related advisory services alongside their voting recommendations. And corporate managers benefit from the wide discretion that stakeholder-oriented commitments afford. Other incentives may reinforce these: avoiding confrontations with activist investors, the reputational benefits of visible sustainability commitments in settings such as the World Economic Forum, the social and professional norms within which many executives and directors operate, and bias against people of faith. Together, these incentives help explain why corporations would adopt net zero commitments without documented support for their returns, despite well-documented concerns about affordability, national security, and energy independence.>>> More Than Ever, It’s Time for Economic Freedom, Not DEI or ESGAll the foregoing also helps explain low vote counts on anti-ESG proposals. Once you’ve accounted for the influence of conflicted asset managers, proxy advisors, and corporate insiders—and public pension funds whose voting policies may weigh collateral policy objectives alongside beneficiaries’ financial interests—there aren’t many votes left that can reflect the views of the “true owners.” As Jerry Bowyer, also mentioned in Wilson’s article, has essentially noted, if a foreign country’s national election returned 2% or less of the votes in favor of a candidate widely known to only have 50% of the support, all the defenders of democracy would be calling the election corrupt and illegitimate.Yet this is basically what we see in proxy voting every season when it comes to conservative anti-ESG and anti-DEI proposals. Vote totals can also be misread in the other direction. When an anti-DEI proposal receives 2% support, the result is sometimes reported as showing that 98 percent of shareholders ‘support DEI.’ Yet comparable pro-DEI proposals have recently drawn similarly low support, particularly since asset managers revised their voting policies and proxy advisors came under regulatory scrutiny. That pattern suggests low totals often reflect reluctance to support prescriptive proposals of either kind, not an endorsement of the underlying policy.All the foregoing helps explain why Heritage believes rescinding Rule 14a-8 too quickly would turn laudable federalism into problematic favoritism by sealing in conflicted gains just when free-market proponents have started making material gains getting corporations back to neutral. And that position can be completely consistent with also supporting the ultimate rescission of the rule due to it being unauthorized and undermining proper federalism.Much more can, should, and will be said about the proper balance of state oversight of proposal submission and scope requirements, as well as federal oversight of related corporate disclosures in interstate commerce. But for now, it is worth noting that a consistent theme animates Heritage’s past and present positions on Rule 14a-8. Heritage certainly appreciates the ways we are witnessing private ordering, federalism, and the marketplace of ideas operating in response to the proposed rescission of the rule, but we are in fact happy “with the SEC’s direction of travel.”.

In a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission. But according to the Global Carbon Budget 2025, the United States accounts for roughly 13 percent of global fossil CO₂ emissions, compared with about 32 percent for China and 8 percent for India. Even if every U.S. corporation reached net zero, the effect on global emissions, and so on the physical risks companies face, would be modest without comparable action elsewhere. Demand for a product does not justify supplying it at any price, and sustainability commitments deserve the same discipline. Their costs and benefits should be fully disclosed so that clients and shareholders can make informed judgments.

According to recent reports, finally, one would expect companies making substantial sustainability commitments to have done the relevant expected-value analysis and to track the returns. Yet even advocates of corporate sustainability acknowledge that this rarely happens. If these conventional justifications are incomplete, a further explanation lies in the incentives of the parties involved. Asset managers market ESG products and compete for mandates from clients who want them. Proxy advisors have offered ESG-related advisory services alongside their voting recommendations. And corporate managers benefit from the wide discretion that stakeholder-oriented commitments afford. Other incentives may reinforce these: avoiding confrontations with activist investors, the reputational benefits of visible sustainability commitments in settings such as the World Economic Forum, the social and professional norms within which many executives and directors operate, and bias against people of faith. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On October 12, 2026, U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), gave a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland in which he outlined NATO’s newly introduced theory of victory to deter and, if necessary, defeat Russian aggression.[REF] This theory of victory, called “Block, Blunt, Break,” centers on employing combined arms and maneuver to block initial enemy assaults on Alliance territory, blunt follow-on offensives, and, if necessary, break the enemy’s ability to sustain combat operations. SACEUR’s speech comes at a time of considerable consternation in Eastern European capitals after months of suspected Russian hybrid activities including drone incursions and sabotage. General Grynkewich’s deterrence-focused theory of victory struck the right tone, reassuring worried allies and signaling to Moscow that the United States and its NATO allies are confident of their ability to defeat a Russian incursion into a NATO state and that Russia would do well not to consider one. The speech and the strategy itself also appear wisely designed to avoid unnecessary escalation with Russia as SACEUR made clear throughout that NATO is a defensive Alliance.Block, Blunt, BreakGeneral Grynkewich stated that a classified version of this new NATO strategy had been agreed on by all 32 members of the Alliance about three months before his October 12 speech.[REF] He explained his decision to present Block, Blunt, Break in public as a helpful measure to assuage increasingly anxious NATO populations vulnerable to evolving security threats.[REF] General Grynkewich summarized his theory of victory as follows: “We will block the initial attack. According to recent reports, on October 12, 2026, U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), gave a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland in which he outlined NATO’s fresh theory of victory to deter and, if necessary, defeat Russian aggression.[REF] This theory of victory, called “Block, Blunt, Break,” centers on employing combined arms and maneuver to block initial enemy assaults on Alliance territory, blunt follow-on offensives, and, if necessary, break the enemy’s ability to sustain combat operations. SACEUR’s speech comes at a time of considerable consternation in Eastern European capitals after months of suspected Russian hybrid activities including drone incursions and sabotage. General Grynkewich’s deterrence-focused theory of victory struck the right tone, reassuring worried allies and signaling to Moscow that the United States and its NATO allies are confident of their ability to defeat a Russian incursion into a NATO state and that Russia would do well not to consider one. The speech and the strategy itself also appear wisely designed to avoid unnecessary escalation with Russia as SACEUR made clear throughout that NATO is a defensive Alliance.

According to recent reports, general Grynkewich noted that a classified version of this new NATO strategy had been agreed on by all 32 members of the Alliance about three months before his October 12 speech.[REF] He explained his decision to present Block, Blunt, Break in public as a helpful measure to assuage increasingly anxious NATO populations vulnerable to evolving security threats.[REF] General Grynkewich summarized his theory of victory as follows: “We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us.”[REF].

This theory of victory is a marked shift from earlier NATO theories of victory, which focused on trading space for time—that is, allowing Russian forces to move into NATO territory, while NATO forces harass and slow Russian advances until decisive force can be brought to bear to destroy and then expel all Russian forces from NATO territory.

Block, Blunt, Break is a significant change from NATO Cold War strategy.

During the Cold War, West Germany was the NATO state considered most likely to be attacked by massive numbers of Soviet-led Warsaw Pact forces, and the Fulda Gap was often identified as the most likely attack route. The geographic size of West Germany meant that NATO forces could fall back tens or hundreds of kilometers before they could generate enough combat mass to begin a counteroffensive against Soviet and Warsaw Pact forces and then expel them from NATO soil. In this sense, NATO planned to trade territory for time, during which it would seize the conventional advantage.

Today, the Suwalki Gap between Lithuania and Poland is often cited as the modern equivalent of the Fulda Gap, especially because it separates Russian-allied Belarus from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.[REF] The three Baltic States of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are for numerous reasons the NATO states against which full-scale Russian aggression is most likely; for example, Russian revanchists claim the existence of Russian-speaking minorities in Estonia and Latvia as a potential pretext, and Russian military planners could seek to connect the Russian exclave by land to either Belarus or Russia, and Lithuania is in their way. In the Baltic States, Block, Blunt, Break makes sense as the strategy for deterring or defending against Russian aggression from both a military planning and a political perspective.

In a recent development, from a military planning perspective, the lack of strategic depth in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania was likely a major factor in the change in strategy. Blocking the Russian advance from the outset prevents the Russians from gaining a foothold that may prove difficult to dislodge once fortified and reinforced.

From a political perspective, Block, Blunt, Break reinforces allied cohesion in the face of Russian aggression against a Baltic state or some other frontline state. Should Russia rapidly gain lodgment within Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, it could then sue for peace before NATO could dislodge Russian forces and liberate those three NATO members. This could well create real political divisions within the North Atlantic Council, in which some countries would press for the liberation of the Baltic States, while others may seek to accept the peace proposal. It is not inconceivable that such a development could lead to the fracturing and potential breakup of NATO—long a goal of Moscow. This new strategy articulated by SACEUR could be a way to defend every inch of NATO soil from the outset and prevent this difficult scenario.

Latest Update: Who supervises the system? Agentic AI and the future of lawyer oversight

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that by Scott A.
  • For two years, the legal profession’s artificial intelligence conversation has centered on an attorney asking a system a question and checking its answer.
  • According to recent reports, systems entering legal practice perform work: taking in a matter, researching, drafting motions, and choosing their own next steps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that by Scott A. Meyers and Michael Adler.

For two years, the legal profession’s artificial intelligence conversation has centered on an attorney asking a system a question and checking its answer. That is no longer enough.

According to recent reports, systems entering legal practice perform work: taking in a matter, researching, drafting motions, and choosing their own next steps. Used well, they can reduce routine work, freeing lawyers for judgment and client advice.

According to recent reports, the profession built its supervision framework around people and bounded tools. An agentic system fits neither model: It has no license to lose or judgment to train, yet acts across a workflow with autonomy the Model Rules do not squarely address.

When AI moves from answering questions to executing multistep legal workflows, what does meaningful human oversight look like?

The unit of supervision is no longer an answer; it is a system of delegated decisions.

Recent findings suggest that the ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct anticipated part of this shift. In 2012, the ABA changed Rule 5.3’s title from “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistants” to “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance.” Its comments encompassed technology-enabled services; a companion resolution added technological competence to what became Comment 8 of Rule 1.1. In 2024, Formal Opinion 512 applied Rules 1.1, 5.1, and 5.3 to lawyers’ use of generative AI and their supervision of the people and providers using it.

That guidance remains organized around a tool: review its output, protect client information, train users and assess providers. It offers less direction when the system executes the workflow, deciding which documents to pull, which facts matter, and what goes where—decisions the finished product may not reveal. Reviewing only the output confirms the car arrived, not its route. Supervision of output is not supervision of process.

METR’s May 2026 report sharpens the point. Assessing agents inside frontier developers (or entities that train AI models), it found them exceeding intended bounds and misleading customers about their work, especially on difficult tasks. It did not study law firm deployments, and routine monitoring might have caught every incident because an independent record existed. The lesson: A lawyer cannot treat an agent’s account as the record of its work. That account is another output of the same probabilistic process, which has training incentives that can reward telling users what they want to hear. Asking the agent to double-check itself is not an independent control.

It has been revealed that accountability cannot rest solely with whoever pressed “run.” It must be institutional and individual, extending to those who designed, approved and maintained the workflow. Every deployed workflow should have a named lawyer-owner authorized to pause it, just as every matter has a responsible partner. This does not displace the matter lawyer’s responsibilities. The owner’s authority must permit suspension on suspicion alone before a committee convenes or a vendor responds. Ownership without it is a label.

It has been revealed that final output review remains necessary. Oversight must also cover consequential junctures: privilege calls, external communications, filings and anything irreversible or beyond client authorization. Supervision begins at design time: deciding what a workflow may do independently, its latitude to reason, and where it must stop and ask. Every firm should be able to answer: Where can this system act without a human seeing it first, and who decided that?

According to recent reports, A tested record on comparable work can justify less intensive routine checking, though never at those consequential junctures. Greater autonomy should be approved and recorded. Material changes to the model, tools, permissions or workflow should trigger reassessment and renewed authorization.

Autonomy bundles three permissions requiring separate calibration: generating work product, accessing sensitive information, and acting in firm or client systems. Permissions should narrow as consequences grow: broad room to draft; matter-scoped room to read; and narrow, logged room to act. A first-year may draft the memo; nobody gives them unilateral wire authority. The grant of action is never implied by the grant of access.

Industry observers note that if a firm cannot trace what a system did, it cannot supervise it; where reasoning cannot be audited, behavior must be. Otherwise, recordkeeping, preservation, and verification of representations to clients, courts, and third parties may suffer. Three mechanisms matter: an audit trail independent of the agent’s reporting, means to interrupt workflows mid-run, and a path to unwind reversible actions—with honesty about those that cannot be reversed. Record model versions and configurations too: Providers update continuously, and a workflow validated in March may differ from August’s.

In a recent development, five workflows can be governed individually; 500 cannot. Solo and small practices may use a simple inventory but still need a way to stop a workflow. At scale, governance becomes operational infrastructure: an inventory of deployed systems, risk classification, approval gates, monitoring and reassessment. The profession knows this playbook: Ask a managing partner how conflicts are governed, and you will hear about a system, not a policy.

Delay accumulates governance debt: workflows deployed faster than they can be inventoried, permissions granted faster than they can be reviewed. Like all debt, it compounds quietly. When data-protection regimes preceded settled enforcement guidance, prudent organizations built from regulatory intent rather than waiting for caselaw. Agentic AI presents the same problem: established duties but no settled operating model.

Ownership, calibrated oversight, permission limits, traceability, reversibility and governance at scale matter wherever organizations deploy agentic AI. What distinguishes law is that our supervisory duties are explicit and long-standing. We are not a special case. We are an early test case.

Fortunately, the test is familiar. Lawyers have been supervising work they did not personally perform since the first associate billed their first hour. The question is no longer only whether lawyers can use AI competently. It is whether we can supervise systems that increasingly do the work of the supervised.

Scott A. Meyers is the chairman and CEO, and Michael Adler is the director of artificial intelligence governance and data protection at Akerman, an Am Law 100 law firm.

The purpose of these columns is to offer practical guidance for attorneys on how to run their practices, provide information about the latest trends in legal technology and how it can help lawyers work more efficiently, and strategies for building a thriving business.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In 1954, the economist Darrell Huff published How to Lie with Statistics, a slim volume that became, improbably, one of the best-selling statistics books in American publishing history.
  • Especially in the wake of a upcoming report, Capturing the Diversity Benefit, which claims that companies with more racially diverse management teams perform better financially.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1954, the economist Darrell Huff published How to Lie with Statistics, a slim volume that became, improbably, one of the best-selling statistics books in American publishing history. Huff’s central insight—that correlation dressed in the vestments of causation can seduce even careful readers—has aged better than most mid-century paperbacks. It’s due for a revival.Especially in the wake of a upcoming report, Capturing the Diversity Benefit, which claims that companies with more racially diverse management teams perform better financially.The report is not without ambition. It draws on federal EEO-1 workforce filings matched to financial data for 1,482 publicly traded companies between 2016 and 2024, and it contains some genuine quantitative analysis.But its empirical research design is deeply flawed, and in ways Huff would have recognized instantly. The analysis may document correlations inside a selected dataset, but it does not establish that management diversity improves corporate performance, that DEI programs create shareholder value, or that companies incur financial risk by scaling those programs back.Consider, first, the sample, always the place a skeptical reader should look, and always the place such reports hope one will not. The number of observed companies changes substantially by year, reaching 1,059 workforce observations in 2020 and falling to 523 in 2024. Earlier data combine voluntary disclosures with records obtained through a Department of Labor Freedom of Information Act release. Later data rely heavily on voluntary disclosure alone, a shift roughly analogous to switching, mid-poll, from a mandatory census to a call for volunteers.>>> DEI’s Days in the Corporate World Are NumberedThe report itself concedes the consequence: companies choosing to disclose had 4.5 percentage points more BIPOC management representation than companies that never disclosed. Selection into the sample is therefore entangled with the very variable under study, which is a polite way of saying the study measures, in part, itself.Nor does the report tell readers how its companies compare with the Russell 3000 or the CRSP-Compustat universe, the benchmarks against which any claim to represent “corporate America” must be tested. Readers do not learn whether the sample differs in size, industry, age, profitability, exchange listing, geographic exposure, or prior stock performance.These are not incidental details; they are precisely the characteristics that predict both workforce composition and financial outcomes. Pooling a large technology company with a small regional manufacturer and regressing profits on a single demographic measure does not make those differences disappear. It merely makes them invisible.The changing sample, moreover, weakens whatever trends the report reports. An average can move for two quite different reasons: because the same firms changed, or because different firms wandered into and out of the dataset. To its credit, the report acknowledges that sample composition may explain part of the sharp decline in female representation it reports for financial services between 2020 and 2021.That caveat, once granted, applies throughout the time series, a fact the report is less eager to grant. A balanced panel and a decomposition of within-firm change from sample entry and exit are prerequisites, not refinements, for interpreting these averages as corporate trends rather than statistical artifacts of who happened to show up.Measurement supplies a second problem, and a subtler one. EEO-1 filings are more standardized than ordinary ESG ratings, which is a modest compliment, but they still require decisions about establishments, corporate ownership, mergers, missing filings, and the aggregation of executive, senior, first-line, and mid-level managers. The report provides too little information to reproduce those choices. Its Racial Justice Initiative score is even less transparent. It combines 27 indicators—ranging from promotion data and EEO-1 disclosure to public statements, donations, and references to political movements—with some categories assigned five times the weight of others. One is invited to trust the recipe without seeing the kitchen.The ESG measurement literature explains, with some precision, why these choices matter. Florian Berg, Julian Kölbel, and Roberto Rigobon compared six major ESG rating systems and found correlations ranging from 0.38 to 0.71, hardly the tight clustering one would expect if these systems were measuring the same underlying reality. They attribute 56% of rating divergence to measurement, 38% to scope, and 6% to weighting.Any claimed DEI-performance relationship therefore raises a prior question, one the report never quite gets around to asking: What DEI score is being used, which indicators enter it, and how are they weighted? A composite social score cannot be treated as an objective corporate trait without its coding rules, missing-data procedures, reliability checks, and sensitivity to alternative weights. Put simply, DEI and ESG scores vary so markedly across providers that they have largely lost their meaning as fixed facts about a company.Related research by Christos Makridis and Majeed Simaan demonstrates that this measurement noise is not merely an academic nuisance; it has real consequences for actual investment decisions. Using more than 22,000 firm-year observations and 21 years of out-of-sample portfolio tests, they find that portfolios incorporating Refinitiv ESG scores do not consistently outperform return-based strategies on a risk-adjusted basis. ESG-only rules can produce higher average returns in some specifications, true enough, but they also generate greater volatility and downside risk (the fine print investors are seldom shown).Return-based factor models achieve comparable or better ex-post ESG standing without using ESG ratings directly at all. Their panel analysis also finds that market volatility predicts later ESG ratings, while ESG ratings do not predict later volatility, suggesting the ratings absorb information the market already knew rather than furnishing anything so useful as foresight.Capturing the Diversity Benefit then commits its largest error, and here Huff would surely have reached for his red pen: it estimates simple bivariate regressions. Financial performance depends on firm size, book-to-market ratios, profitability, investment, leverage, industry, firm age, prior performance, and macroeconomic conditions. The main analysis controls for none of them. This omission is especially damaging because the report’s own tables show sharply different results across market-capitalization groups. The authors call firm size “almost certainly” a confound—then proceed, undeterred, to present unadjusted aggregate estimates anyway.Income after tax, measured in dollars, illustrates the difficulty. Large companies generally earn more dollars and may also employ more diverse managers. A positive coefficient can therefore capture company scale rather than operating performance—correlation masquerading, once again, as insight.Raw multiyear stock-price appreciation is similarly inadequate to the task. Finance researchers evaluate abnormal returns only after accounting for established sources of risk and return. The Fama-French five-factor model incorporates market exposure, size, value, profitability, and investment; cross-sectional work commonly employs the Fama-MacBeth method to test whether a given characteristic predicts returns after competing explanations have had their say. The report employs none of this.Timing presents yet another serious obstacle. Matching workforce composition in a given year with performance measured in that same year does not reveal which came first. Strong companies may simply have more resources to recruit broadly, invest in management systems, and publish workforce data in the first place. Both diversity and performance may reflect nothing more exotic than management quality itself. Showing that a correlation existed before 2020 does not resolve the question of reverse causality. It merely pushes it back a few years. At a minimum, the analysis should use lagged representation to predict future outcomes, control for prior performance, and account for the swath of unobserved differences across firms over time.The report also runs hundreds of statistical tests across demographic groups—approximately 15 outcomes, 11 sectors, three size categories, and nine years. At a 5% significance threshold, false positives become not merely possible but inevitable when researchers search across that many combinations. It would be more surprising if nothing turned up significant by chance alone. Yet the tables display only plus signs, minus signs, and blanks. They omit coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals, and economic magnitudes—the very information a reader would need to judge whether “significant” means “large” or merely “detectable.” The analysis should identify a small set of primary outcomes and adjust for multiple testing accordingly.Prior research illustrates why this quantitative discipline matters so greatly. Jeremiah Green and John Hand attempted to reproduce McKinsey’s influential diversity-performance findings using observable S&P 500 data and found no statistically reliable relationship between executive racial and ethnic diversity and industry-adjusted profitability, sales growth, return on assets, return on equity, or total shareholder return. Their critique also identifies reverse causality in relating later diversity measures to earlier performance—the chicken-and-egg problem dressed in academic clothing.>>> The Myth of “Voluntary” ESGAlex Edmans, Caroline Flammer, and Simon Glossner draw an equally crucial conceptual distinction. Their employee-survey measure of DEI has little correlation with demographic representation as such. It is associated with stronger future accounting performance, earnings surprises, and valuation ratios while demographic diversity, on its own, is not. The DEI measure also does not predict future stock returns. Representation, inclusion, and corporate programs are, in short, different constructs measuring different things, and the report moves among them with a freedom the evidence does not license.Which raises the damning question: if DEI scores do not reliably reflect a company’s actual demographic composition, doesn’t the entire argument collapse under its own premise?None of this forecloses the possibility that a serious analysis might yet find that management diversity contains financially relevant information. The current report has simply not demonstrated it. The authors should compare their sample with the public-company universe, publish their data construction and coding rules, use a balanced panel, estimate models with firm and year fixed effects, control for standard company characteristics, evaluate factor-adjusted returns, lag the workforce variables, and correct for multiple testing. In 1954, the economist Darrell Huff published How to Lie with Statistics, a slim volume that became, improbably, one of the best-selling statistics books in American publishing history. Huff’s central insight—that correlation dressed in the vestments of causation can seduce even careful readers—has aged better than most mid-century paperbacks. It’s due for a revival.

Especially in the wake of a upcoming report, Capturing the Diversity Benefit, which claims that companies with more racially diverse management teams perform better financially.

It has been revealed that the report is not without ambition. It draws on federal EEO-1 workforce filings matched to financial data for 1,482 publicly traded companies between 2016 and 2024, and it contains some genuine quantitative analysis.

But its empirical research design is deeply flawed, and in ways Huff would have recognized instantly. The analysis may document correlations inside a selected dataset, but it does not establish that management diversity improves corporate performance, that DEI programs create shareholder value, or that companies incur financial risk by scaling those programs back.

Recent findings suggest that consider, first, the sample, always the place a skeptical reader should look, and always the place such reports hope one will not. The number of observed companies changes substantially by year, reaching 1,059 workforce observations in 2020 and falling to 523 in 2024. Earlier data combine voluntary disclosures with records obtained through a Department of Labor Freedom of Information Act release. Later data rely heavily on voluntary disclosure alone, a shift roughly analogous to switching, mid-poll, from a mandatory census to a call for volunteers.

These are not incidental details; they are precisely the characteristics that predict both workforce composition and financial outcomes. It merely makes them invisible.

An average can move for two quite different reasons: because the same firms changed, or because different firms wandered into and out of the dataset. That caveat, once granted, applies throughout the time series, a fact the report is less eager to grant. One is invited to trust the recipe without seeing the kitchen.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there were two springs, back when my brother and I were still boys of that gawky middle-school age, when my grandparents, Nina and Papa, gathered us up and carried us west. I have come to think of those two trips as a single, long unspooling of memory.The first took us to Arizona. We saw the Grand Canyon, that impossible gash in the earth, and the Painted Desert beyond it, striped like something bruised and beautiful. We bounced along in the backs of jeeps that kicked up desert dust. We stayed at a hotel in Flagstaff, where the mornings came on white with snow and the afternoons turned hot and dry as a stovetop, as though the day couldn’t decide what season it wanted to be.The second spring we went to Jackson Hole, to the Tetons standing up out of the earth like something out of scripture, and there we stayed in a log cabin, where the rangers warned us, upon arrival, of a moose grown ill-tempered from guests who wouldn’t leave him be. Naturally, I took this admonition as an invitation. While Nina sat rocking on the porch, drinking in the view with a contentment only a woman of her years could summon, I crept beneath the floorboards and began to stomp and snort and generally conjure, as best I understood it, the sound of an enraged and antlered beast.She shrieked; I laughed.>>> Poe, the Pandemic and a Halloween Lesson for Catholics and ProtestantsFrom there we went to Yellowstone, to Old Faithful and the moose that actually behaved themselves. I remember, at the geyser, an old man off to the side smoking a pipe, the smoke curling up thin and blue against all that steam, and Papa remarking, almost wistfully, on how good it smelled. Nina noted he ought to have one himself if he wanted it so badly, then waved the thought away before it could take root.It was only later that I learned the truth of it: that Papa had given up his pipe before his own sons were born—my uncles, twins, identical down to the part in their hair—because he hadn’t wanted them growing up believing it an admirable habit. This was long before anyone had made a campaign of such things. He had simply decided it, alone, the way men of his generation did, and never smoked again.We went white-water rafting down the Snake River, my brother and I giddy with anticipation, having not yet learned to factor our grandparents’ ages into our adventures. It turned out to be less a plunge through rapids than a gentle float past serene banks, the water flat and shining as poured glass. And it was later that day, pulled over at some highway overlook to admire the view, that the bikers came: a great, leather-clad, tattooed gang of them, thundering up out of nowhere until it was only them and us. My brother and I did the arithmetic of our own mortality and did not like the sum.But Nina—devout as she was, pious in a manner that never once announced itself—had already seen the little fish symbol stamped on one of the motorcycles, and before either of us could stop her, she was walking straight toward them, unhurried, as if she’d been expecting them all along. We were certain she would die.>>> A Very Merry Southern ChristmasInstead, within moments, she was praying with them, the whole rough, tattooed circle of them bowed together on the roadside, and then there was laughter, and embracing, and finally—this being the age of disposable cameras—photographs, Nina beaming in the middle of hairy, greasy men who just before had looked to us like the end of the world.That photograph exists somewhere still, I have to believe, though my grandmother died last year, and it has not yet turned up.Adam Smith, in closing his Theory of Moral Sentiments, observed something of how swiftly we render our verdicts upon strangers, how a glance, a coat, a scar, a rough voice, can convict a man in an instant, long before he has said a word in his own defense. It’s sympathy alone, he thought, that corrects the error, the strange and sudden capacity to feel our way into another’s situation and find, waiting there, not the stranger we feared but the neighbor we hadn’t yet recognized.I think of my grandmother on that roadside, walking toward the very thing my brother and I had already convicted, carrying no evidence but a small fish stamped in chrome—and finding exactly what Smith promised was always there to be found, if only someone was brave enough, or faithful enough, to go looking for it before the verdict came.

There were two springs, back when my brother and I were still boys of that gawky middle-school age, when my grandparents, Nina and Papa, gathered us up and carried us west. I have come to think of those two trips as a single, long unspooling of memory.

According to recent reports, the first took us to Arizona. We saw the Grand Canyon, that impossible gash in the earth, and the Painted Desert beyond it, striped like something bruised and beautiful. We bounced along in the backs of jeeps that kicked up desert dust. We stayed at a hotel in Flagstaff, where the mornings came on white with snow and the afternoons turned hot and dry as a stovetop, as though the day couldn’t decide what season it wanted to be.

The second spring we went to Jackson Hole, to the Tetons standing up out of the earth like something out of scripture, and there we stayed in a log cabin, where the rangers warned us, upon arrival, of a moose grown ill-tempered from guests who wouldn’t leave him be. Naturally, I took this admonition as an invitation. While Nina sat rocking on the porch, drinking in the view with a contentment only a woman of her years could summon, I crept beneath the floorboards and began to stomp and snort and generally conjure, as best I understood it, the sound of an enraged and antlered beast.

She shrieked; I laughed.

>>> Poe, the Pandemic and a Halloween Lesson for Catholics and Protestants.

Sources indicate that from there we went to Yellowstone, to Old Faithful and the moose that actually behaved themselves. I remember, at the geyser, an old man off to the side smoking a pipe, the smoke curling up thin and blue against all that steam, and Papa remarking, almost wistfully, on how good it smelled. Nina stated he ought to have one himself if he wanted it so badly, then waved the thought away before it could take root.

It was only later that I learned the truth of it: that Papa had given up his pipe before his own sons were born—my uncles, twins, identical down to the part in their hair—because he hadn’t wanted them growing up believing it an admirable habit. This was long before anyone had made a campaign of such things. He had simply decided it, alone, the way men of his generation did, and never smoked again.

In a recent development, we went white-water rafting down the Snake River, my brother and I giddy with anticipation, having not yet learned to factor our grandparents’ ages into our adventures. It turned out to be less a plunge through rapids than a gentle float past serene banks, the water flat and shining as poured glass. And it was later that day, pulled over at some highway overlook to admire the view, that the bikers came: a great, leather-clad, tattooed gang of them, thundering up out of nowhere until it was only them and us. My brother and I did the arithmetic of our own mortality and did not like the sum.

But Nina—devout as she was, pious in a manner that never once unveiled itself—had already seen the little fish symbol stamped on one of the motorcycles, and before either of us could stop her, she was walking straight toward them, unhurried, as if she’d been expecting them all along. We were certain she would die.

>>> A Very Merry Southern Christmas.

Instead, within moments, she was praying with them, the whole rough, tattooed circle of them bowed together on the roadside, and then there was laughter, and embracing, and finally—this being the age of disposable cameras—photographs, Nina beaming in the middle of hairy, greasy men who just before had looked to us like the end of the world.

That photograph exists somewhere still, I have to believe, though my grandmother died last year, and it has not yet turned up.

Sources indicate that adam Smith, in closing his Theory of Moral Sentiments, observed something of how swiftly we render our verdicts upon strangers, how a glance, a coat, a scar, a rough voice, can convict a man in an instant, long before he has noted a word in his own defense. It’s sympathy alone, he thought, that corrects the error, the strange and sudden capacity to feel our way into another’s situation and find, waiting there, not the stranger we feared but the neighbor we hadn’t yet recognized.

I think of my grandmother on that roadside, walking toward the very thing my brother and I had already convicted, carrying no evidence but a small fish stamped in chrome—and finding exactly what Smith promised was always there to be found, if only someone was brave enough, or faithful enough, to go looking for it before the verdict came.
