    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that today the Department of Justice confirmed coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.
    • It has been revealed that “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” noted Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M.
    • It has been revealed that “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” mentioned Assistant Attorney General A.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that today the Department of Justice confirmed coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.

    It has been revealed that “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” noted Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement indicates that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”.

    It has been revealed that “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” mentioned Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division quickly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.”.

    Industry observers note that “Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” mentioned First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure reveals that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”.

    “By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” remarked U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.”.

    “The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” stated FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”.

    “North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” said Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.”.

    Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California.

    Sources indicate that today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California revealed the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain.

    North Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.

    During the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the new victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts.

    The North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.

    Recent findings suggest that the FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.

    Recent findings suggest that the effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

    The Department, FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen From Binance.

    Separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

    Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.

    The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and the IRS-CI.

    November 23, 2026, 10:03 am CST.

    In a recent development, in an effort to help overburdened federal courts, a bipartisan group of U.S. senators reintroduced a bill Friday that would add 71 newly introduced federal judgeships in phases over several presidential administrations. (Image from Shutterstock).

    According to recent reports, in an effort to help overburdened federal courts, a bipartisan group of U.S. senators reintroduced a bill Friday that would add 71 new federal judgeships in phases over several presidential administrations.

    Congress last enacted a significant expansion of the federal courts in 1990, according to a story by Law360.

    The federal courts currently have 677 district judgeships and 179 appellate judgeships. Under the bill, judgeships would be added in a number of states, including Arizona, California, Iowa, Newly introduced Jersey and New York.

    In a recent development, the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate passed a version of the bill in 2024, but then-President Joe Biden vetoed it during his last few weeks in office.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, forty-six years ago today, the Supreme Court issued its ruling in Stone v. Graham, holding that a Kentucky statute requiring a copy of the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms violated the First Amendment’s establishment clause because it “has no secular legislative purpose.” That 1980 ruling is back in the spotlight this term, as the court considers whether to take up challenges to similar Ten Commandments laws in Texas and Louisiana.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court denied review in dozens of cases, including two DEI-related disputes – the first, a challenge from University of California scholars to cuts in research funding; the second, a challenge from California doctors to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses – and a Second Amendment clash over Maryland laws prohibiting guns in “sensitive places.”.

    The court also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks.

    For more on Monday’s order list, see the Morning Reads and On Site sections below.

    The December session of oral arguments will begin on Nov. 30.

    #101518. The U.S. Navy is retiring the peacoat—the kind that Robert Redford wore in Three Days of the Condor

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (687 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    The U.S. Navy is retiring the peacoat—the kind that Robert Redford wore in Three Days of the Condor

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome to The Fashion Police, a column where we spotlight some of the best fashion in crime film and TV.
    • It has been revealed that it’s true.
    • They are replacing it with a black, synthetic, all-weather parka.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to The Fashion Police, a column where we spotlight some of the best fashion in crime film and TV.

    It has been revealed that it’s true. The United States navy is retiring a its signature peacoat. Yes, its signature peacoat! “The double-breasted, hip-length wool peacoat that is synonymous with the romance of the sea.” They’re retiring an iconic garment, a staple not only of military fashion, but also of fashion in general.

    They are replacing it with a black, synthetic, all-weather parka. Why are they doing this? A statement from the Navy’s Uniform Board mentioned that it was due to the Navy’s “commitment to eliminating unnecessary costs while ensuring sailors have the cold-weather protection they need to accomplish their missions.” The U.S. Naval Institute News revealed that it was chosen was chosen for its “modern appearance,” and “its versatility in being able to be worn with service and dress uniforms and civilian clothing.” But it has NO personality. This is like tearing down a historic 18th century townhouse to put up a glass and steel high rise.

    In her piece on this landmark decision, Vanessa Friedman at The Latest York Times noted the history and symbolic associations of the garment, writing.

    Sources indicate that first designed for Dutch sailors in the 18th century, the pijakker was particularly well-suited for life at sea: roomy enough to accommodate warm inner layers but streamlined enough not to get caught in a ship’s rigging. Its collar could be turned up to shield the face against wind, and side pockets kept the coat closer to the body in cold weather.

    Adopted by the Royal Navy in 1857, the peacoat made the leap to the U.S. Navy shortly thereafter, becoming standard issue in 1886. And though small details may have been tweaked, the general style has remained the same.

    According to recent reports, in 1962, Friedman notes, Yves Saint-Laurent included a peacoat in his womenswear Rive-Gauche show, launching the coat as as style staple for women. According to the brand,.

    In a recent development, the simple shape of this practical garment sculpted the silhouette. The fact that it was not fitted and covered the hips made it ideal for women who did not yet feel daring enough to wear pants, which accentuated the female form.

    Saint Laurent’s 1962 fashion show opened with the pea coat, which was the first piece he presented under his own name. The model wore it with white shantung pants and mules. This ensemble paved the way for Yves Saint Laurent’s signature style, which borrowed from menswear in order to make women feel comfortable and confident.

    Sources indicate that but, for our purposes, the most iconic use of the peacoat is Robert Redford’s look in Three Days of the Condor, Sydney Pollack’s 1975 political espionage thriller, based on James Grady’s novel Six Days of the Condor). Redford plays a low-level CIA employee in Fresh York City who is the sole survivor of an attack on his small office branch, and then goes on the run, attempting to untangle what appears to be an enormous intra-bureau conspiracy. The peacoat is a nice choice for this character; as Valerie Steele, the director of the Museum at the Fashion Institute of Technology told The New York Times, “the peacoat doesn’t have the associations with violence and warfare often attached to camouflage and Army greatcoats. Rather, the peacoat more often represents bravery against the elements and the romance of voyages to places unknown.”.

    Industry observers note that olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. Her other work appears in Vanity Fair, Vulture, Lapham's Quarterly, AirMail, the Los Angeles Review of Books, Public Books, The Baffler, Bright Wall/Dark Room, Politics/Letters, The Toast, Truly Adventurous, and elsewhere. She has a PhD from the departments of English/comparative literature and theatre at Columbia University, where she was the Marion E. Ponsford fellow.     Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Two of the most enduring rights in the Constitution are the First Amendment’s protections of the free exercise of religion and the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause.
    • 3, several of the conservative justices in their questions suggested that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down.
    • Colorado, in 2024, adopted a universal preschool program where it will provide funds for children to attend public, secular private, or faith-based preschools.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Two of the most enduring rights in the Constitution are the First Amendment’s protections of the free exercise of religion and the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause. Should the court’s approach to these rights vary? Specifically, should it be easier to prove discrimination under the free exercise clause than under equal protection?

    At the oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, on Nov. 3, several of the conservative justices in their questions suggested that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down. That is in sharp contrast with a half century of law under equal protection holding that disparate impact (seemingly neutral policies that result in negative effects on a particular group) is not enough to prove discrimination. I would not be surprised to see such “free exercise exceptionalism” from the Roberts court. But it seems to me unjustified.

    In a recent development, st. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy.

    Colorado, in 2024, adopted a universal preschool program where it will provide funds for children to attend public, secular private, or faith-based preschools. The condition for receiving funds is that the school must consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.”.

    Recent findings suggest that st. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colorado, which has a Catholic preschool, and two parents brought a challenge arguing that this restriction on funding violates their free exercise of religion as it requires them to accept students whose families do not adhere to the Catholic Church’s teachings, including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents. The federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit upheld the Colorado law.

    The 10th Circuit stressed that the Colorado law did not discriminate on the basis of religion. The court applied the Supreme Court’s 1990 decision in Employment Division v. Smith, which held that the free exercise clause cannot be used to challenge a neutral law of general applicability. This means that the free exercise clause is not a basis for an exception to a law unless it can be shown either that it was motivated by a desire to interfere with religion, that it discriminates against religion, or even that it just creates discretion to treat religions differently from secular actions. The 10th Circuit found that the Colorado law met the requirements for a neutral law of general applicability, as, among other things, it did not treat any one religion differently than others.

    Industry observers note that the court of appeals also found no discrimination against religious schools in government funding. In 2017’s Trinity Lutheran v. Comer, the court declared unconstitutional a Missouri law that provided public and secular private schools funds for surfacing playgrounds that did not provide the same funds to religious schools. In 2022’s Carson v. Makin, the court applied this to invalidate a Maine law that provided funds to parents to send their children to secular private schools in areas without public schools, but not “sectarian” schools. The 10th Circuit distinguished these cases, explaining that the Colorado law did not exclude religious schools as it allowed them to receive state money on the same terms as all other preschools.

    At the oral argument on Nov. 3, there was more focus on the latter matter, perhaps because it would avoid the court needing to decide whether to overrule Employment Division v. Smith. In 2021’s Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, Justice Samuel Alito wrote an opinion concurring in the judgment, joined by Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch, urging the overruling of Smith. Justice Amy Coney Barrett, joined by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, wrote a concurring opinion, expressing support for that view, but finding it unnecessary to decide the issue to resolve that case. The court likely remains divided over whether to overrule Smith and what would replace it.

    According to recent reports, in the arguments in St. Mary Catholic Parish, there were many questions from the conservative justices that suggested that they saw the Colorado law as discriminatory because of its effects on religious schools. For example, Chief Justice John Roberts asked the attorney for Colorado how this was different from the program in Carson v. Makin and noted that the effect of the Maine law was “pretty much the same as the effect of the law here,” as it disadvantaged religious schools. Barrett asked Colorado’s attorney why, if Colorado cannot expressly exclude religious schools from its program, it can nevertheless “impose a condition” – the nondiscrimination requirement – that it knows such “schools will be unable to agree to.”.

    It has been revealed that in other words, these justices suggested that a discriminatory effect of Colorado’s law would be sufficient to find the law violated the free exercise of religion even though the law remarked nothing about religion and was not motivated by a desire to interfere with religion. The questions suggested that Colorado adopting the non-discrimination requirement knowing that some religious schools would not comply should be sufficient to prove discrimination under the free exercise clause.

    Such an approach would be dramatically different from analysis under the equal protection clause. Although I personally think such cases were incorrectly decided, the Supreme Court long has held that proof of a discriminatory effect alone is not sufficient to establish race or sex discrimination. And it has expressly held that discrimination cannot be proven by showing that government officials took an action with knowledge that it would have discriminatory consequences.

    Sources indicate that washington v. Davis, decided 50 years ago, was a key case holding that a racially discriminatory effect is not sufficient to establish an equal protection violation. Applicants for the police force in Washington, D.C., were required to take a test, and statistics revealed that Black individuals failed the examination much more often than Whites. The Supreme Court, however, held that proof of a discriminatory impact is insufficient, by itself, to show the existence of a racial classification. Justice Byron White, writing for the majority, noted that the court never had held that “a law or other official act, without regard to whether it reflects a racially discriminatory purpose, is unconstitutional solely because it has a racially disproportionate impact.” The court explained that discriminatory impact, “[s]tanding alone, . . . does not trigger the rule that racial classifications are to be subjected to the strictest scrutiny and are justifiable only by the weightiest of considerations.”.

    It has been revealed that the court has even held that discriminatory purpose cannot be proven by showing that government officials adopted a policy with knowledge that it would have a discriminatory effect. Rather, the court has made it clear that showing such a purpose requires proof that the government desired to discriminate. In 1979’s Personnel Administrator of Massachusetts v. Feeney, the court declared: “‘Discriminatory purpose,’ … implies more than intent as volition or intent as awareness of consequences. It implies that the decisionmaker . . . selected or reaffirmed a particular course of action at least in part ‘because of,’ not merely ‘in spite of,’ its adverse effects upon an identifiable group.”.

    Feeney involved a challenge to a Massachusetts law that gave preference in hiring for state jobs to veterans. At the time of the litigation, more than 98% of the veterans in the state were male, and only 1.8% were female. The result was a substantial discriminatory effect against women in hiring for state jobs. Nonetheless, based on the principles articulated above, the Supreme Court held that there was not a sex classification because the law creating a preference for veterans was facially sex neutral and there was not proof that the state’s purpose in adopting the law was to disadvantage women. The fact that the legislature knew there would be an discriminatory effect against women was thus irrelevant.

    Industry observers note that there is no way to reconcile this equal protection jurisprudence with the approach several conservative justices suggested in St. Mary Catholic Parish. The question then becomes whether there is any reason to treat discrimination under the free exercise clause differently from under the equal protection clause.

    Sources indicate that several justices suggested in their questions at oral argument that Sherbet v. Verner, a 1963 case, justifies concluding that discriminatory impact is alone sufficient for a free exercise violation. That case involved a state having denied unemployment benefits to a woman, a member of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, who quit her job rather than work on her Saturday Sabbath. The court concluded that the denial of benefits imposed a substantial burden on religion; the woman had to choose between an income and her faith. The court thus remarked that the problem was “whether some compelling state interest enforced in the eligibility provisions of the . . . statute justifies the substantial infringement of appellant’s First Amendment right.” The court found no such compelling interest and ruled that the denial of benefits constituted a violation of the free exercise clause.

    Sources indicate that sherbert found a violation of the free exercise of religion based on the impact on her religion despite the law at issue being facially neutral. As a precedent for striking down the Colorado law, however, that is unpersuasive. Sherbert was decided a decade before the Supreme Court held that proof of discriminatory impact was not sufficient for an equal protection violation. And although the court has not overruled Sherbert, it has never explained how it can be reconciled with Employment Division v. Smith. But most importantly, invoking Sherbert begs the crucial question: Should a different standard be used for discrimination under the free exercise clause compared to the equal protection clause?

    Conceptually, I cannot understand any reason why discrimination on the basis of religion should be treated dissimilarly from discrimination based on race or sex. Why should two such critical rights be treated differently? Indeed, it is just a doctrinal accident that religious discrimination is litigated under the free exercise clause (or the establishment clause) rather than the equal protection clause.

    According to recent reports, applying equal protection principles, the Colorado law does not discriminate against religion in its terms or in its purpose. Many commentators, including me, have argued that – despite court precedent – discriminatory impact should be enough for a claim under equal protection. But there has been no suggestion from the court that it is moving in that direction.

    It has been revealed that finally, it is important to stress that even if the law is deemed discriminatory, that does not mean that it is automatically unconstitutional. It means that strict scrutiny should be applied, in which the government action can be upheld if there is a compelling purpose for it. I was disappointed that the conservative justices did not focus on the government’s compelling interest in preventing children from being discriminated against on account of their gender identity or for having LGBTQ parents. Without explicitly saying so, the justices appear poised to carve out a special place for the free exercise clause over that of equal protection.

    According to recent reports, erwin Chemerinsky is the Dean and Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law, University of California, Berkeley School of Law.

    In a recent development, recommended Citation: Erwin Chemerinsky, Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently , SCOTUSblog (Nov. 17, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/treating-the-free-exercise-of-religion-and-equal-protection-differently/.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that A federal jury in the Eastern District of New York returned guilty verdicts following a three-month trial against Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. (Huawei) and three of its subsidiaries for violating U.S. sanctions involving Iran, lying to banks, money laundering, and stealing trade secrets from American companies. As proven at trial, Huawei and several of its subsidiaries, including Chinese subsidiary Huawei Device Co. Ltd. (Huawei Device) and U.S. subsidiaries Futurewei Technologies Inc. (Futurewei) and Huawei Device USA Inc. (Huawei Device USA), engaged in a decades-long scheme to enrich Huawei and grow its telecommunications business, including in the United States, through criminal activities.

    “No person or firm is above the law,” remarked Attorney General Todd Blanche. “For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft. Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable.”.

    “For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft, and deception,” mentioned Assistant Attorney General Tysen A. Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security. Today’s verdict sends an unmistakable message: America will defend its businesses, protect its workers, and safeguard its national security against corrupt foreign corporations that lie, cheat, and steal to get ahead.”.

    “Huawei violated our laws, empowered our enemies, and harmed our national security,” mentioned Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “This conviction highlights that the National Security Division and its partners will not rest until companies like Huawei are held to account for their bad conduct in an American court of justice.”.

    “Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” mentioned U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of Latest York. “Today’s verdict is a step towards accountability for Huawei’s criminal activities, which includes yearslong collaboration with sanctioned entities in Iran, repeated lies to banks, and blatant thefts from U.S. technology companies.”.

    It has been revealed that “For years, Huawei and its subsidiaries carried out an egregious campaign to expand their international enterprise through theft of trade secrets, fraud, and other criminal conduct at the expense of U.S. companies and the rule of law,” stated Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “This case serves as a stark reminder that the Chinese government continues to pose a serious threat to our economic and national security, but today’s guilty verdict proves the FBI and our partners will aggressively investigate, expose, and hold accountable those who target our nation. No company is too major, too powerful, or too well connected to exploit the U.S. and its citizens and expect to escape American justice.”.

    Industry observers note that huawei and its subsidiaries assisted the government of the Islamic Republic of Iran by providing turnkey services with respect to an internet backbone and broader accessibility for mobile networks in the country. Huawei also helped the Iranian regime and a component of the Iranian intelligence apparatus, Zaeim, to monitor and censor its owners’ access to the internet. Testimony further established that Huawei provided surveillance cameras that enabled the Iranian regime to monitor protest activity.

    It has been revealed that huawei conducted its business in Iran under the name “Skycom.” Huawei repeatedly lied about the nature of its business in Iran, falsely telling banks, journalists, and the U.S. government that it did not assist Iran’s government, military, or intelligence community; that it began restricting its business in Iran in 2011; that Skycom was a business partner, rather than a wholly-owned subsidiary; and that Huawei complied with all applicable sanctions. Huawei knew that all of those statements were materially false and misleading.

    In a recent development, huawei lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and access to U.S.-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services — in part because of its lies.

    It has been revealed that the jury convicted Huawei and three subsidiaries of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), substantive violations of IEEPA, and money laundering conspiracy. When sentenced, the defendants face financial penalties including criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution. Sentencing has been set for Sept. 14, 2027. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

    The investigation is being conducted by the FBI’s New York Field Office.

    Trial Attorneys Taylor G. Stout, Morgan Cohen, and Jasmin Salehi Fashemi of the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF), Trial Attorney Aaron L. Jennen of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section, and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Alexander A. Solomon, Meredith A. Arfa, Robert M. Pollack, Matthew Skurnik, and Matthew F. Sullivan for the Eastern District of New York (EDNY) are prosecuting the case, with assistance provided by Assistant U.S. Attorney Brendan G. King, EDNY paralegal specialists Matthew Jennings and Grace Yang, and MNF paralegal specialists Christina Roman, Alexa Stiles, Heather DePremio, Jackson Mayo, and Angela R. Ancalle Jiménez.

    According to recent reports, MNF’s mission is to take the profit out of crime, eliminate drug cartels, and protect the U.S. financial system. MNF pursues criminal prosecutions and criminal and civil asset recovery actions involving: financial facilitators who launder profits for criminals; financial institutions and their officers and employees whose actions threaten the U.S. financial system and financial institutions; international money launderers who support transnational organized crime; and the top command and control of international drug trafficking organizations.

    MNF’s Bank Integrity Unit investigates and prosecutes banks and other financial institutions, including their officers, managers and employees whose actions threaten the integrity of the individual institution or the wider financial system.

    #101511. Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1578 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing.
    • Until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a).
    • It has been revealed that under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Oct. 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing. This question now sits at the court in two pieces: a statutory question the justices have agreed to answer, and a constitutional one still waiting for the right case. Together, the answers will decide whether people who have lived here for years, even decades, can ask a judge to release them while they fight deportation.

    Until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a). According to this provision, ICE may release a detainee on bond subject to an immigration judge’s review (unless Section 1226(c)’s criminal- and terrorism-related provisions apply). In July 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement began requiring – for the first time – that anyone who had entered the United States without inspection, whether last year or decades ago, be detained instead under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) for the length of removal proceedings. Unlike Section 1226(a), this provision holds that immigration judges have no power to grant such detainees bond. Two months later, the Board of Immigration Appeals agreed with ICE in Matter of Yajure Hurtado.

    It has been revealed that under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit. Partly due to this policy, ICE’s overall detained population, which also includes people held on other grounds, hit a reported record of roughly 73,000 in mid-January 2026.

    Sources indicate that section 1225(a)(1) deems any noncitizen “present in the United States who has not been admitted [to the country]” to be an “applicant for admission.” The detention command then provides: “in the case of an alien who is an applicant for admission, if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained.” The courts of appeals agree that long-term residents who entered the U.S. unlawfully are deemed “applicant[s] for admission.” The dispute is whether that deemed status also means they are “seeking admission,” and would thus fall within Section 1225 and be detainable without bond.

    Eleven of the 12 federal circuit courts (all but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit) have now answered. Nine hold that Section 1226, not Section 1225(b)(2)(A), governs people arrested in the interior: the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th, 9th, 10th and 11th Circuits. Two read Section 1225(b)(2)(A) as the government does: the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 5th Circuit and the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 8th Circuit.

    For the majority of circuits, “seeking admission” is an ordinary phrase Congress left undefined, and as the 1st Circuit put it, “means seeking lawful entry.” A person who crossed the border years ago is not seeking entry; he already entered. The deeming clause in Section 1225(a)(1) may make a long-term resident an applicant for admission, Judge Joshua Kolar wrote for the 7th Circuit, but it does not “conjure a fictional intent to seek admission.” Structure points the same way: in the Laken Riley Act of January 2025, Congress expanded Section 1226(c)’s mandatory detention categories to reach certain unlawful entrants accused or convicted of specified offenses, a needless step if Section 1225 had always reached them. The majority of circuits add that five administrations over three decades read the statute their way, and that Congress would not silently have required detaining some two million people.

    For the 5th and 8th Circuits, however, ordinary meaning cuts differently. To apply for something is to seek it, Judge Edith Jones wrote for the 5th Circuit; for example, a college applicant does not stop seeking admission once the application is filed. Several dissenters elsewhere go further and rest on the deeming clause itself, arguing that a legal fiction carries the attributes of the thing it deems. As 11th Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa wrote in dissent, in a line later adopted by a 1st Circuit dissenter: “If a person whom Congress has deemed an applicant for admission is not seeking admission, it is hard to know what Congress thought it was deeming him to be.”.

    Recent findings suggest that as for the government’s long contrary practice: “Years of consistent practice,” Jones wrote, “cannot vindicate an interpretation that is inconsistent with a statute’s plain text.” Government-side judges answer the Laken Riley point, too: Section 1226(c) also reaches admitted noncitizens and bars parole, and in January 2025 DHS still treated unlawful entrants as bond-eligible. Both sides now also cite the justices’ own June decision in Mullin v. Al Otro Lado, which read “arrives in the United States” to mean crossing the border, said fears of encouraging illegal entry “cannot defeat the best reading of the text,” and called the rule that every word must do work “not an iron rule.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Supreme Court will soon have its say. On Oct. 1, the justices agreed to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, the government’s challenge to a unanimous 2nd Circuit panel ruling for a Brazilian man who has lived here more than 20 years, was detained in 2025 under Section 1225(b)(2)(A), and which that circuit court found to be inapplicable. No argument date is set yet; proposed merits briefing runs into February, pointing to argument in late winter or spring and a decision by term’s end.

    Industry observers note that but a related constitutional question is also pending at the court. This is whether, even if under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) detainees do not have a statutory right to a bond hearing, they have a right to one under the due process clause. On Oct. 23, the full U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit held in the case of Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara that noncitizens subject to the government’s mandatory detention policy have no such right.

    Industry observers note that judge Cory Wilson wrote for the majority: “Because Petitioners have never been admitted to the United States, due process does not entitle them to additional proceedings beyond what Congress has provided before they may be detained pending removal.” Seven judges dissented. Judge Leslie Southwick countered that the court “has constructed an impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents,” who by the record had each lived here for more than a decade.

    According to recent reports, for now, in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi, noncitizens who entered without inspection thus have no ordinary path to a bond hearing; discretionary parole and a few claims the majority reserved remain, but those are narrow exits. The 8th Circuit’s ruling closes the statutory route across its seven states as well.

    The 3rd and 6th Circuits, on the other hand, have held that detaining long-present noncitizens under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) without a bond hearing does indeed violate due process. In these circuits, which cover Delaware, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and the U.S. Virgin Islands (the 3rd Circuit), and Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and Tennessee (the 6th Circuit), long-term residents can point to circuit precedent recognizing a due process right to a bond hearing. One’s geographical location thus makes all the difference.

    If the court affirms in Rhoney, subject to specific exceptions, noncitizens who entered without inspection and are later arrested in the interior could again ask for bond everywhere, as they could before July 2025. A hearing does not guarantee release, and the burden is generally on the detainee, but the right to ask for bond would be the same in every circuit. If the court reverses in Rhoney, mandatory detention becomes the statutory rule everywhere, yet geography, as noted, would still matter: the 3rd and 6th Circuits have held that a constitutional right to due process requires bond hearings for long-resident detainees like those before them, and the 5th has held it does not.

    Sources indicate that that is where the case of Putra v. Lopez-Campos comes in. The government’s petition from its loss in the 6th Circuit in that case raises both the statutory and constitutional questions, and the solicitor general urged the justices to take it for that reason. The court only agreed to hear Rhoney, which raises the statutory question, and thus appears to be holding Putra until Rhoney is decided. If the government wins in Rhoney, the split between the 3rd and 6th Circuits, which found a due process right to a bond hearing, and the 5th, which did not, would matter far more, and the justices would likely have to take up Putra to settle the due process concern. But if the detainees win in Rhoney, that constitutional question may never need an answer.

    Rhoney should be decided before the term ends next summer. Based on this decision, we will see if the constitutional dispute follows. In the meantime, tens of thousands of people remain detained.

    Kemal Hepsen is the managing attorney of Hepsen Law Firm, a federal litigation firm that represents noncitizens nationwide in habeas corpus, mandamus, and Administrative Procedure Act cases.

    #101509. Justices to consider disputes over transgender servicemembers, E. Jean Carroll’s jury award, and acting U.S. attorneys at next private conference

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (986 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Justices to consider disputes over transgender servicemembers, E. Jean Carroll’s jury award, and acting U.S. attorneys at next private conference

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on latest petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks.
    • The federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec.
    • Talbott, the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on latest petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks. But when they do, on Friday, Dec. 4, they will have a number of high-profile cases to consider – which could, in turn, lead to a busy spring.

    The federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec. 4.

    In United States v. Talbott, the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.

    In the government’s petition for review, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit “gravely erroneous” and argued that its “reasoning cannot be squared with this Court’s precedents or deference to the military.”.

    The challengers urged the court to stay out of the dispute, calling the D.C. Circuit’s decision “narrow” and temporary. And in any event, they added, the ruling is correct, because the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers was motivated by hostility to transgender people rather than “military judgments.”.

    It has been revealed that in another case to be considered, Trump and the federal government have each filed petitions for review in connection with Trump’s challenge to the $83.3 million verdict entered against him in a lawsuit brought by E. Jean Carroll, who had alleged that in 1996 Trump had sexually abused her in a dressing room at a Upcoming York department store and that Trump in 2019 had defamed her by calling her a liar.

    Trump’s petition for review points to the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States, in which it held that presidents generally have broad immunity for their acts while in office. Trump’s private attorney, Robert Giuffra, wrote that “[t]he threat of even a single damages judgment based on official acts will render all Presidents ‘unable to boldly and fearlessly carry out [their] duties for fear that [they] may be next.’”.

    The federal government’s petition for review asks the Supreme Court to also decide whether the federal government, rather than Trump, should be the defendant in Carroll’s case because Trump made the statements at the center of the dispute as part of his role as president.

    It has been revealed that and in United States v. Jackson and United States v. Office of the Latest York State Attorney General, the justices will decide whether to weigh in on the legality of Trump’s appointments of acting U.S. attorneys in Nevada and New York.

    It has been revealed that under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, the federal law that governs how the executive branch can temporarily staff vacant positions that require presidential appointment and confirmation by the Senate, interim officers can serve for 120 days. Under that law, then-Attorney General Pamela Bondi appointed Sigal Chattah as the interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada, effective April 1, 2025, after Jason Frierson, who was nominated by then-President Joe Biden, stepped down.

    In a recent development, with only a few days remaining before her interim appointment was set to expire, Chattah resigned, and Bondi designated her as the first assistant U.S. attorney. In that post, Bondi remarked, Chattah would have the power under the FVRA “to serve as Acting United States Attorney upon a vacancy in that office.” Bondi also gave Chattah the powers of a U.S. attorney for legal proceedings in Nevada.

    Recent findings suggest that bondi followed a similar path for John Sarcone in the Northern District of New York, naming him first as the interim U.S. Attorney and then, when his interim term expired, naming him as the first assistant U.S. attorney and a “special attorney,” effectively designating him as the “Acting U.S. Attorney.”.

    When challenges to the legitimacy of Chattah’s and Sarcone’s appointments followed, lower courts agreed that neither had been validly appointed. Sauer then came to the Supreme Court, where he told the justices that Chattah’s appointment was not only lawful, but “a critical tool that the Executive Branch has used without meaningful objection for 25 years.” He urged the court to take up that case, and to hold the New York case until the Nevada case is resolved.

    Recent findings suggest that in addition to those disputes, the justices will consider three other noteworthy petitions for review on Dec. 4:.

    One thing to keep in mind: although the justices are slated to vote on these cases for the first time on Dec. 4, they may not act on any of them right away. In particular, for several years, the court has had a general practice of not granting a petition for review until the justices have considered it at two conferences. After the Dec. 4 conference, the justices will meet again on Dec. 11.

    Industry observers note that finally, yet another high-profile petition for review is likely to be before the justices soon: Trump v. Clinton, in which Trump is seeking to revive his lawsuit against Hillary Clinton (and several others, including the Democratic National Committee) alleging “a coordinated scheme … to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion.” Clinton originally waived her right to file a response to Trump’s petition, but the court called for a response, which she filed on Nov. 13. In her response, Clinton contends that “President Donald Trump and his attorneys” “attempt to frame a routine opinion disposing of a frivolous lawsuit as a threat to ‘the Presidency.’”.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    #101504. An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1324 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences.
    • In a recent development, iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct.
    • Industry observers note that the state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences. But the significant shift towards Democrats in states previously controlled by Republicans is likely to impact immigration law even sooner. The Supreme Court is presently considering whether to add to its calendar a case about the constitutionality of an immigration law enacted by Iowa in 2024. The justices had previously signaled their openness to weighing in, but the state’s Republican attorney general, who asked the court to hear the case, lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, casting doubt on the case’s future.

    In a recent development, iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct. For example, anyone who has previously been excluded or deported from the United States by federal immigration officials but “is at any time found” in Iowa can be convicted of an aggravated misdemeanor and imprisoned for up to two years. As an alternative to potential conviction, the law allows a state judge overseeing a criminal prosecution to order the defendant to leave the United States. Anyone who fails to leave as required can be convicted of a felony and imprisoned for as much as 10 years.

    Industry observers note that the state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law. The Immigration and Nationality Act permits criminal prosecution of migrants who are found in the United States after having previously been removed. It also allows immigration judges to order a migrant to depart the United States. By resembling federal law, Senate File 2340’s proponents hoped to assist the federal government’s efforts to penalize and remove from the United States people who had violated federal immigration law.

    According to recent reports, in two separate lawsuits, challengers questioned the law’s constitutionality. An advocacy group based in Des Moines, the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, and two Iowa residents who had previously been removed from the United States filed one lawsuit, while the Justice Department, during President Joe Biden’s tenure, filed the other. In June 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa sided with the challengers in both cases. Since Senate File 2340 regulates immigration, it treads on an area of law that is the responsibility of the federal government, U.S. District Judge Stephen Locher concluded. As the Supreme Court explained in a 2012 decision, Arizona v. United States, involving Arizona’s attempt to enact its own immigration laws, “The federal power to determine immigration policy is well settled.”.

    According to recent reports, in addition, any time that Congress enacts legislation in an area in which it is authorized to do so, including immigration, the supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution prioritizes federal law over state law. “Under this principle, Congress has the power to preempt state law,” the Supreme Court explained in Arizona. By enacting a detailed, complicated set of immigration laws, including criminal offenses related to migration, “Congress ‘left no room’ for state regulation” of migration, Locher explained. Since Senate File 2340 attempts to regulate migration, it is likely preempted. Locher thus blocked Iowa from enforcing it.

    Within days, Iowa’s attorney general, Republican Brenna Bird, appealed the district court’s decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit. While the case was pending before the 8th Circuit, President Trump returned to the White House, and the Justice Department asked the district court to dismiss its lawsuit. Despite the federal government’s shifting position, Senate File 2340 did not fare well before the 8th Circuit. Deciding Bird’s appeal of the case brought by the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two Iowa residents, the circuit court concluded that each section of Senate File 2340 conflicts with federal immigration law and is therefore likely preempted.

    Having lost at the 8th Circuit, Bird asked the Supreme Court to weigh in. Iowa’s law should be allowed to go into effect because it merely “mirrors federal law,” Bird told the justices in her request for review last July. Unsurprisingly, Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two residents who challenged the law urged the justices not to add this case to their calendar. They argued that the 8th Circuit applied the law in line with other federal courts that have grappled with similar disputes, so the court’s intervention is unnecessary.

    Last month, the justices signaled that they were more interested in this case, Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, than most others vying for their attention. On Oct. 19, the court invited the solicitor general – the federal government’s top lawyer before the Supreme Court – to explain whether the Trump administration thinks the court should become involved. Calling for the solicitor general’s view is a key sign that the justices are closely considering whether to add the case to their calendar. Of the thousands of cases that the court is asked to review every year, the justices request the solicitor general’s view in a small handful – “around 10 or 11 times every term,” according to SCOTUSblog contributor John Elwood. For that reason, invitations to the solicitor general “serve as powerful signals that a petition has attracted the court’s serious attention,” Elwood explained.

    It has been revealed that the solicitor general has not yet responded to the court’s invitation, but there is reason to believe it will ask the court to grant Iowa’s request – or would have absent this month’s electoral swing. By voluntarily dismissing its lawsuit last year, the Trump administration removed the federal government from stopping Iowa’s enforcement of Senate File 2340. Since then, it has left no doubt that it stands with Iowa. After the 8th Circuit concluded that Iowa could not enforce the law, the Justice Department urged the full court to rehear the case and side with Iowa. “[T]he panel opinion misapplied preemption principles to affirm the district court’s preliminary injunction,” the Justice Department told the 8th Circuit in an amicus brief that it filed in the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice’s case.

    But the results of this month’s elections may have dimmed the prospects of Supreme Court review. Bird lost her reelection bid to Democrat Nate Willems. Though Willems has not publicly taken a position on Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340, in an interview he accused her of having “filed too many of what I think of as political lawsuits.” He instead noted he would focus on “times when there is a real threat to Iowans or a real harm,” and promised to boost the attorney general’s work on behalf of consumers, workers, and the environment. Willems’ Democratic colleague Rob Sand won the state’s gubernatorial election. Sand also has not publicly explained his position on Senate File 2340, but with Democrats holding two of the highest offices in state government, they are likely to align with each other.

    In a recent development, once sworn in as Iowa’s next attorney general, Willems will be able to move forward with or drop Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340. Under the court’s rules, a case will be dismissed when both parties agree. Since Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the state’s two residents who challenged the law have indicated that they do not want the court to intervene, all that is left is for Willems to make his view known. Having already lost in two courts, Senate File 2340 remains alive only thanks to Bird’s insistence that those judges misunderstood the state’s role in punishing migrants. But if he wants, Willems can turn the attorney general’s office’s attention to other matters, providing yet another reason why elections matter.

    César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández is the author of three books about immigration law and policy.

    #101499. The Supreme Court before it stood apart

    The Supreme Court before it stood apart

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1586 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A.
    • In her excellent new book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.
    • Sources indicate that that will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A. Shelden (The University of North Carolina Press).

    In her excellent new book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.

    Sources indicate that that will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court. But Shelden’s history demonstrates that the 19th century court and the way Americans perceived it were very different. Indeed, the modern idea of the detached judge, the justice as apolitical “umpire,” is not nearly as originalist as we tend to assume.

    According to recent reports, shelden opens with Abraham Lincoln arguing before the court in 1849. The court that Lincoln and his fellow members of the bar knew was not the marble institution, removed from ordinary political life, that we picture today. For example, the justices “rode circuit.” Each was assigned a region, generally the part of the country from which he hailed and in which he traveled through to preside over federal trial courts. This brought the justices into regular contact with local lawyers, officials, and communities.

    In a recent development, shelden calls this “judicial representation”: the idea that a justice would bring a region’s perspective to the court because he knew the people he impliedly represented. Although today’s justices are assigned to a circuit, typically the circuit to which they have ties geographically, the concept is now decidedly different; except at certain prescheduled events, justices no longer directly communicate with the people in that circuit as part of their duties, but handle applications from it in the corridors of the marble palace. “Judicial representation” is most definitely no longer a thing.

    But this just scratches the surface of the differences that Shelden lays out. In the 19th century, the justices were active participants in the political debates of their time, in ways that today would not only be grounds for profound criticism but even potential impeachment.

    In a recent development, chief Justice John Marshall was himself an active participant in such discourse. In 1800, before becoming chief, Marshall began contributing to the Washington Federalist, a newspaper established to support President John Adams and later oppose Thomas Jefferson. Marshall’s involvement was so extensive that he became known as the brains behind the paper. Nor did his appointment to the court entirely sever his connection to it. Elias Caldwell, the Supreme Court’s clerk during Marshall’s tenure, subsequently became its proprietor. The paper remained staunchly Federalist under Caldwell’s leadership, regularly attacking the Jefferson administration’s policies as unconstitutional.

    Marshall’s political opponents suspected that he continued to exert considerable influence behind the scenes at the Washington Federalist even as chief justice, directing those attacks. Indeed, the Philadelphia Aurora, a newspaper aligned with Jefferson, described Caldwell as “a creature of John Marshall, chief justice.” Shelden casts doubt on Caldwell’s denial of Marshall’s involvement. And given that Caldwell was Marshall’s own clerk at the Supreme Court, you can understand the skepticism.

    In a recent development, justice William Johnson provides another example. In 1823, Johnson ruled (in his lower-court circuit-riding role) that South Carolina’s Negro Seamen Act, which authorized the detention of free Black sailors arriving in Charleston, violated the Constitution. Local officials were furious and refused to publish his opinion in the newspapers. So Johnson took his argument directly to the public, putting his opinion in a pamphlet that was circulated around the country, and then supporting the decision via pseudonymously authored op-eds that submitted his interpretation of the Constitution was correct.

    Nor were the justices’ newspaper writings limited to defending their decisions. In 1848, Justice John McLean published letters addressing such political issues as the national bank, taxation, infrastructure, and the Mexican-American War, all while his supporters were encouraging him to pursue the presidency.

    According to recent reports, and in 1859, Justice John Catron publicly opposed proposed Tennessee legislation that would have enslaved free Black residents who remained in the state. Catron used his connections at the Nashville Union and American to publish a letter criticizing the legislation. The newspaper’s editors attacked his position, producing a public back-and-forth in its pages. Catron’s letter was even reprinted in Missouri, where similar legislation was under consideration. Tennessee ultimately rejected the proposal, and Shelden suggests Catron’s intervention may have mattered.

    To put this in perspective, such actions would be akin to Justice Clarence Thomas writing an opinion piece in The Wall Street Journal defending the Republican Party’s position on disputed legislation, or Justice Elena Kagan publishing an article in The Latest York Times supporting a Democratic president’s legislative agenda.

    Yet the justices’ political involvement went well beyond expressing opinions publicly. Some actually ran for elected office while continuing to serve on the court.

    Shelden recounts the example of Justice Smith Thompson, who accepted the nomination for governor of Fresh York in 1828 while a justice. Thompson ultimately lost to Martin Van Buren by more than 30,000 votes. After losing the election, Thompson simply continued serving on the court, where he remained for another 15 years.

    Justice McLean, meanwhile, was discussed as a potential presidential candidate in the 1830s, with political allies contemplating his nomination even as he continued hearing cases. Indeed, both McLean and his colleague, Justice Levi Woodbury, would later emerge as presidential contenders in 1848.

    Justice William Johnson, appointed by President Thomas Jefferson, actually won election as a commissioner of the poor in Charleston Neck, South Carolina, in 1826. In this role, he exercised authority over local taxation, patronage, and public resources. Johnson held this elected position, and won reelection, while continuing to serve on the Supreme Court.

    Again, by way of comparison, imagine Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson declaring herself a candidate for the 2028 presidential election – while continuing to decide cases and write opinions. Or contemplate Justice Neil Gorsuch simultaneously holding an elected local government office with taxing authority.

    According to recent reports, just as notable was the willingness of justices to involve themselves directly in the work of the other branches of government. In doing so, they corresponded with presidents and members of Congress about public policy. They even offered advice on legislation and, in some instances, helped craft it.

    Recent findings suggest that during Reconstruction, Chief Justice Salmon Chase pressed President Andrew Johnson on Black suffrage and used his political relationships to influence Reconstruction policy. For his part, just a few years earlier, Justice John Campbell of Alabama sought to influence President-elect Lincoln to issue a public statement reassuring Southern moderates that his administration would not interfere with slavery in their states. Campbell even offered to publish a letter in his own name, as a citizen of Alabama, to help create an occasion for Lincoln to make such a statement.

    When Lincoln declined to act, Campbell turned to President James Buchanan. He urged Buchanan to send commissioners to the secession conventions to persuade the delegates to preserve the Union. Campbell’s efforts ultimately failed. But consider what he was doing: a sitting Supreme Court justice was privately advising both an incoming and an outgoing president about how to address the most consequential political crisis in the nation’s history.

    Now imagine Chief Justice John Roberts privately consulting with President Donald Trump about birthright citizenship, or Justice Sonia Sotomayor advising former President Joe Biden about his unconstitutional student loan forgiveness program and how it could be fixed.

    In a recent development, in the dénouement of the book, Shelden traces how the political world of the justices changed as the 19th century drew to a close. Circuit riding ended, the legal profession grew more formal, and the court became more centered in Washington. As the country marked the Constitution’s centennial, lawyers and judges helped tell a new story of the court, one that made political detachment seem like some sort of longstanding tradition. (To be fair, this did not bring such political involvement to an immediate end.).

    If I have one criticism of Shelden’s otherwise excellent work, it is that she doesn’t explore this transformation in nearly the same depth as she does the earlier history. How, exactly, did the justices (and their fellow Americans) come to accept a view of the court so different from the one they had held for much of the 19th century, and which we hold today? That is a fascinating question in its own right, and perhaps the worthy subject of a follow-up volume.

    According to recent reports, regardless, Shelden’s history offers a challenge to today’s justices, as well as to proponents and critics of the modern court. Nineteenth-century justices participated much more freely in political life, while today’s justices insist that they must stand apart from politics, even as many Americans cast a dubious side eye upon that claim. Was it better when justices did not deny the political world they inhabited and were a part of? And can the way we look at the court, and the way the justices see themselves, change again? I don’t think the answers are obvious. But Shelden’s book made clear to me that a reflexive dismissal of such questions is based more on historical ignorance than any fixed tradition of the Supreme Court as appearing apolitical.

    Mark Miller directs Environment and Natural Resources litigation at Pacific Legal Foundation.
